glmtree: logistic regression trees

glmtree builds decision trees with a logistic regression at each leaf: the tree cuts the population into segments, and each segment gets its own, interpretable, scoring function. The segmentation is searched jointly with the regressions by a stochastic EM algorithm, as described in Formalization and study of statistical problems in Credit Scoring, Ehrhardt A. (see the manuscript or the web article).

Installation 

install.packages("glmtree")                # from CRAN
# development version
# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("adimajo/glmtree")

Example 

library(glmtree)

set.seed(1)
data <- generateData(n = 2000, scenario = "tree")   # 3 segments, 3 different regressions
features <- c("x1", "x2", "x3")

fit <- glmtree(data[, features], data$y, K = 5, iterations = 100,
               ctree_controls = partykit::ctree_control(alpha = 0.1, minbucket = 100, maxdepth = 4))
fit                                                  # number of segments, criterion, the tree
predict(fit, data[1:5, features])                    # probabilities
predict(fit, data[1:5, features], type = "segment")  # segments
fit@best.tree$glms                                   # the logistic regression of each segment

partykit also exports a function called glmtree() (model-based recursive partitioning). If you attach both packages, call ours as glmtree::glmtree(). See vignette("glmtree") for the interface (validation, test, criterion, burn_in, patience, …).

What to expect: measured results

The numbers below come from inst/benchmarks/real_data.R (20 random stratified 70/30 splits per dataset, 100 SEM iterations, K = 5; the full table and the raw results are in inst/benchmarks/results/). They are test-set Gini coefficients (2 AUC - 1, higher is better), means over the splits. Tree-based methods use leaves of at least 5% of the training data and depth 4. glmtree selects the tree with the BIC on the training data, glmtree (valid.) uses 25% of the training data as a validation set and the Gini. MOB is partykit::glmtree(), the model-based recursive partitioning, with all features both as regressors and as partitioning variables.

Dataset logit ctree MOB random forest glmtree glmtree (valid.)
Simulated, 3 segments (n = 3000) 0.248 0.568 0.698 0.657 0.650 0.644
Simulated, 1 regression (n = 3000) 0.672 0.619 0.672 0.606 0.672 0.670
German credit (1000 × 20) 0.552 0.439 0.436 0.579 0.514 0.393
Pima diabetes (532 × 7) 0.704 0.591 0.704 0.665 0.697 0.633
ISLR Default (10000 × 3) 0.896 0.867 0.896 0.849 0.894 0.893
AER CreditCard (1319 × 10) 0.670 0.608 0.654 0.692 0.667 0.668
ISLR Caravan (5822 × 85) 0.439 0.400 0.439 0.426 0.413 0.379

What this says, honestly:

  • glmtree is not a general-purpose accuracy booster. It helps when the population really is made of segments with different regressions: on the simulation with three segments it goes from 0.248 (one logistic regression) to 0.650, using 4.1 segments on average (three are true). On the five real datasets no single-tree method (ctree, MOB, glmtree) beats a plain logistic regression: glmtree is between 0.002 and 0.038 below it, because the data are close to a single regression and the chain mostly keeps one or two segments (1.2 to 1.7 on average). Only the random forest is ahead, on German credit (+0.027 ± 0.007, paired mean ± standard error) and CreditCard (+0.022 ± 0.006).
  • partykit::glmtree() (MOB) is the stronger and faster alternative on these data. On the simulation with segments MOB scores higher than glmtree (0.698 against 0.650) and takes 1.4 s per fit against 11 s. On the real data sets MOB either does not split (it is then identical to the logit: Pima, Default, Caravan) or loses (German credit 0.436, CreditCard 0.654), where glmtree stays close to the logit. glmtree is neither faster nor more accurate than MOB in this benchmark; what it offers is a different, likelihood-based search (a latent segment variable), a choice of criterion (BIC, AIC, held-out Gini) and ctree for the segmentation.
  • The validation set version is the worse choice on small samples (German credit 0.393, Pima 0.633): holding out data makes both the fit and the selection noisy. Prefer the BIC on the training data unless the sample is large.
  • Cost. A fit of 100 iterations takes 3 to 18 s on the data sets above (5 s for 1319 observations, 18 s for 7000 training observations; 160 s for the 85 features of Caravan), measured with six fits running in parallel. About 70% of the time is spent in partykit::ctree, which is refitted at every iteration. Compared with this package’s own version 0.3.1, the rewrite of version 0.4.0 made an iteration about twice as fast for the same accuracy (2.4×, 2.2× and 2.0× for 1000, 3000 and 10000 observations, 50 iterations; inst/benchmarks/speed.R).
  • Convergence is slow in iterations. On the simulation with segments, the test Gini rises with the iteration budget (BIC on the training data, mean over 12 repetitions): 0.639 (25 iterations), 0.645 (50), 0.652 (100), 0.658 (200), 0.664 (400), 0.676 (800), and the best iteration is still far into the chain (349 on average for 800). With patience = 25 the chain stops after about 51 iterations in about 5 s at a Gini of 0.646, against 75 s for 800 iterations: use patience for a quick answer, and a large iterations if the extra 0.03 Gini matters (inst/benchmarks/convergence.R).

Reproduce with Rscript inst/benchmarks/real_data.R 20 100 and Rscript inst/benchmarks/convergence.R (they need partykit, ranger, scorecard, ISLR, AER; about an hour).
